questions.q: Why does grid search scale so poorly with the number of swept parameters?
options: It only supports continuous distributions, not discrete values
It enumerates every combination of discrete values, so adding a parameter multiplies the total run count
It requires a GPU per parameter
Grid search cannot be configured in YAML
questions.explain: Grid search is exhaustive: a grid of 3 values across 2 parameters is 9 runs, and adding a third 3-valued parameter makes it 27. The run count multiplies with each added dimension.

questions.q: According to the Bergstra and Bengio result, when does random search outperform grid search at an equal trial budget?
options: Never — grid search is always at least as good
Only when every hyperparameter matters equally
When only a few hyperparameters actually matter, which is the common case
Only when the search space has exactly two dimensions
questions.explain: Random search's independent sampling of each parameter gives good coverage of each dimension regardless of how many other dimensions are present, which beats grid search's wasted exhaustive coverage of unimportant dimensions.

questions.q: What does Bayesian search use to decide which configuration to try next?
options: A fixed, pre-generated list of configurations in random order
A probabilistic model of how the metric depends on the hyperparameters, balancing exploration and exploitation
The configuration that was used in the most recently completed run
An exhaustive enumeration of the remaining grid cells
questions.explain: Bayesian search builds a probabilistic model (commonly Gaussian-process-based) of the metric surface and chooses the next configuration expected to be most informative, trading off exploring unknown regions against exploiting promising ones.

questions.q: What is the main downside of Bayesian search compared to random or grid search?
options: It cannot optimize continuous hyperparameters
It requires more memory per training run
It is inherently sequential, since each suggestion depends on prior results, so it parallelizes worse
It always requires more total trials than grid search
questions.explain: Because each new Bayesian suggestion depends on the outcomes of previous trials, it is harder to run many trials fully in parallel, unlike random or grid search where every trial is independent.

questions.q: Based on the lesson's rule of thumb, when is Bayesian search the better choice over random search?
options: When you have many parallel workers and want to explore broadly and cheaply
When individual training runs are expensive and parallelism is limited
When the search space has only two discrete values total
When no metric needs to be optimized
questions.explain: Bayesian search's sample efficiency pays off most when each trial is costly (hours or days) and you can't run many trials in parallel — the sequential bottleneck matters less when parallelism was limited anyway.
